title: Temples, Teachers and Chinatown
bigQuestion: How do temples, schools and neighborhoods keep old teachings alive today?

story.title: Why the Lion Bows
story.kicker: A boy in Chicago's Chinatown watches a lion dance stop at every shop door.
paragraphs: Drums boom along Wentworth Avenue in Chicago's Chinatown. It is Lunar New Year. Leo holds his aunt's hand and stands on his toes. A lion with a huge red and gold head dances down the street.
Two dancers are inside the lion. One works the head, and one is the back legs. The lion blinks its big eyes and shakes its fur. Cymbals crash each time it jumps.

Then the lion stops at a bakery door. It bows low, three times. The owner hangs a red envelope and some green lettuce by the door. The lion reaches up, takes them, and scatters the leaves in the street.

"Why does the lion bow at the doors?" Leo asks. His aunt smiles. "It is saying hello with respect," she says. "And it brings good wishes to each shop for the new year. The shop thanks the dancers with the envelope."
story.think: Why might bowing be a good way for the lion to greet each shop?

lessons.title: Confucius's Hometown Temple
lessons.mainIdea: In Qufu, Confucius's hometown, a large temple has honored him for more than 2,000 years.
reading: Confucius was born in a place now called *Qufu* (choo-foo), in eastern China. After he died, people honored him at his old home. Over many centuries, rulers made the site larger and grander.

Today the Temple of Confucius in Qufu has many halls, courtyards and old trees. Its main hall has yellow roof tiles, a color once used for emperors. Stone tablets in the courtyards record gifts and visits by rulers over the centuries.
Near the temple stand the Kong family mansion and the Kong family cemetery. Confucius's family name was Kong. In 1994, UNESCO named the temple, mansion and cemetery a World Heritage Site.

words.d: Confucius's hometown in eastern China, home of the largest Temple of Confucius
a building where people show honor to a teacher, ancestor or holy figure

look.title: Walk Through the Gates
look.text: Picture walking into the Qufu temple. You pass through gate after gate. Old cypress trees line the path. Stone turtles carry tall stone tablets on their backs. At last you reach a great hall with a yellow roof.
look.prompt: Why might a temple make visitors walk through many gates before they reach the main hall?

check.q: Where is Confucius's hometown temple?
check.why: The largest Temple of Confucius stands in Qufu, his hometown in eastern China.

check.q: What was Confucius's family name?
check.why: Confucius's family name was Kong, as in the Kong family mansion.

check.q: What did UNESCO do in 1994?
choices: Named the Qufu temple, mansion and cemetery a World Heritage Site
check.why: UNESCO listed the three Qufu sites as a World Heritage Site in 1994.

lessons.title: A Day for Teachers
lessons.mainIdea: In Taiwan, Teachers' Day falls on Confucius's traditional birthday and opens with a ceremony in his honor.
reading: Confucius is honored as a great teacher. Tradition dates his birthday to about 551 BCE. In Taiwan, September 28 is kept as his birthday. It is also *Teachers' Day*.

Early that morning, a ceremony is held at the Taipei Confucius Temple. Musicians play old instruments. Young dancers move slowly in rows while holding feathers and flutes. Officials offer gifts and bow. This *ceremony* follows steps that are many centuries old.
Around the country, students thank their teachers with cards and flowers. Other places mark the day too. Qufu holds a large celebration each fall. China keeps its own Teachers' Day on September 10.

words.d: a day to thank teachers; in Taiwan it is September 28, Confucius's traditional birthday
a set of planned, formal actions done to mark an important event

look.title: Thank-You Notes
look.text: A fourth grader in Taipei writes a card: "Thank you for helping me read hard words. You never gave up on me." Her classmate brings a flower. Their teacher smiles and pins the card on the board.
look.prompt: Why might a country choose a great teacher's birthday as the day to thank all teachers?

check.q: What day is Teachers' Day in Taiwan?
check.why: Taiwan keeps Teachers' Day on September 28, Confucius's traditional birthday.

check.q: What happens at the Taipei Confucius Temple on that morning?
choices: A ceremony with music, dancers and bows
check.why: An old ceremony with music, slow dancers and offerings honors Confucius that morning.

check.q: Why is Confucius linked to Teachers' Day?
choices: He is honored as a great teacher
check.why: Confucius is remembered above all as a teacher, so his birthday honors teachers.

lessons.title: Daoist Temples and Priests
lessons.mainIdea: Daoist temples are living places where priests lead ceremonies and visitors light incense.
reading: Some temples belong to *Daoism*. Daoism is a Chinese tradition that follows the Dao, or the Way. Many Daoists honor Laozi, the old teacher linked to a book called the Daodejing. Some honor him as a deity.

Step into a Daoist temple and you may smell incense. Visitors light sticks, hold them up, bow and place them in a large pot. Many are asking for health or blessings for family. Statues of deities sit in the halls.

Daoist *priests* wear long robes and often keep their hair in a knot. They chant old texts, play instruments and lead ceremonies for festivals, blessings and funerals. For many families, the temple is part of everyday life.

words.d: a Chinese tradition that follows the Dao, the Way; it has books, temples and priests
a trained leader who performs ceremonies in a religious tradition
a being honored as holy or divine by a tradition

look.title: Lighting Incense
look.text: A grandmother enters a Daoist temple. She lights three sticks of incense from a candle. She holds them up with both hands, bows three times, and places them in a big bronze pot. Smoke rises slowly toward the roof.
look.prompt: What might each of the grandmother's actions show? Describe them without joining in.

check.q: What does the Dao mean?
check.why: Dao means the Way; Daoism is the tradition that follows it.

check.q: Which teacher do many Daoists honor?
check.why: Daoists honor Laozi, linked to the Daodejing; some honor him as a deity.

check.q: What do Daoist priests do?
check.why: Daoist priests chant, play music and lead ceremonies for festivals and funerals.

sections.title: Books at the Heart of School

lessons.title: The Great Exams
lessons.mainIdea: For about 1,300 years, people in China took hard exams on the classics to become government officials.
reading: Imagine a test so important that it could change your whole family's life. In old China, men who wanted government jobs took the *civil-service exams*. These began around 605 CE and ended in 1905.

The exams tested the *classics*. These are old, honored books, like the Analects of Confucius. Students spent years memorizing them and writing essays about them. Test-takers sat alone in tiny rooms for days.
Passing brought honor to a whole family and village. Few passed the highest level. So the classics sat at the heart of schooling for about 1,300 years. That is why Confucius's words spread so widely.

words.d: tests in old China, about 605 to 1905 CE, to choose government officials
old, honored books that people study for a long time, like the Analects

look.title: How Long the Exams Lasted
rows: Zhu Xi's notes on the classics become the exam standard
look.cite: Common dates for China's imperial exams (Sui dynasty to 1905)
look.prompt: Subtract the first year from the second. About how many years did the exams last?

check.q: What were the civil-service exams for?
check.why: The exams chose men for government jobs by testing the classics.

check.q: About how long did the exams last?
check.why: From about 605 to 1905 CE is about 1,300 years.

check.q: What did the exams test?
check.why: Students memorized and wrote about the classics, like the Analects.

lessons.title: Learning Like Confucius
lessons.mainIdea: Confucius taught that learning and practice go together and that anyone can be a teacher to you.
reading: The Analects begins with a question about school. Confucius asks: is it not a joy to learn something and practice it often? He links learning with doing again and again.

Confucius also taught that we can learn from people around us. In Analects, book 7, he says that when he walks with two others, one can surely teach him. He copies their good ways and fixes in himself what is not good.

Students in China, Korea, Japan and Vietnam memorized lines like these. Many families today still say Confucius's ideas shape how much they value school. Others point out that people value learning for many reasons.

words.d: the book of Confucius's sayings, written down by his students
doing something again and again so you get better at it

look.title: Walking With Two Others
look.text: When I walk with two other people, I can surely find a teacher. I follow their good ways, and I change in myself what is not good.
look.cite: Analects 7.21 (7.22 in some editions), retold in simple words from James Legge's translation, 1893
look.prompt: What does Confucius say he can learn from people who are not good?

check.q: How does the Analects begin?
choices: With a story about a lion
With a list of zodiac animals
With the joy of learning and practicing
check.why: Analects 1.1 asks whether it is not a joy to learn and practice what you learned.

check.q: In Analects 7.21, what can Confucius learn from people who are not good?
choices: How to fix the same fault in himself
check.why: Confucius says he changes in himself what he sees is not good in others.

check.q: Who wrote down Confucius's sayings?
check.why: His students and later followers wrote down his sayings in the Analects.

lessons.title: Chicago's Chinatown
lessons.mainIdea: Chicago's Chinatown on the South Side is a busy neighborhood with shops, schools, churches and temples.
reading: Chicago's *Chinatown* sits on the South Side, near Cermak Road and Wentworth Avenue. A big painted gate stands over Wentworth. Bakeries, restaurants, herb shops and bookstores line the streets.
Families live, work and go to school here. There are churches, temples and family associations. Many families have lived in Chicago for generations. Others arrived more recently.

Each Lunar New Year, a *parade* fills Wentworth Avenue. Lion dancers, dragon dancers, drummers and marching bands take part. Thousands of people come to watch, from the neighborhood and from across Illinois.

words.d: a neighborhood where many Chinese and Chinese American families live, work and shop
a line of people, music and floats that moves down a street to celebrate
a dance by two people inside a lion costume, done at New Year to bring good wishes

look.title: A Walk on Wentworth
look.text: You walk under the gate on Wentworth Avenue. You smell fresh egg tarts from a bakery. You pass a shop selling dried herbs in glass jars. A church bell rings nearby. Down the block, people light incense at a temple.
look.prompt: What does this walk show about the many ways people live in Chinatown?

check.q: Where is Chicago's Chinatown?
choices: On the North Side by the lake
On the South Side near Cermak and Wentworth
check.why: Chicago's Chinatown is on the South Side, near Cermak Road and Wentworth Avenue.

check.q: What happens on Wentworth Avenue at Lunar New Year?
choices: A parade with lion and dragon dancers
check.why: Chinatown's Lunar New Year parade fills Wentworth Avenue.

check.q: In the story, why does the lion bow at shop doors?
choices: To greet with respect and bring good wishes
check.why: The lion bows as a respectful greeting and brings New Year wishes to each shop.

lessons.title: Many Ways of Believing
lessons.mainIdea: Many Chinese Americans mix Confucian, Daoist, Buddhist or Christian practice, and some keep no religion at all.
reading: Ask ten Chinese American families about religion and you may hear ten answers. One family goes to a Christian church on Sunday. Another visits a Buddhist temple. Another keeps an ancestor shelf at home.

In China, people often speak of the *three teachings*: Confucian, Daoist and Buddhist. Many people draw on more than one. A family might honor ancestors in a Confucian way and visit a Daoist temple for a blessing.

Some families say they have no religion but still keep Qingming and New Year. Scholars even debate whether Confucianism is a religion. Some call it a way of life. The best way to learn is to listen to each family.

words.d: Confucian, Daoist and Buddhist ways of thought, which many people in China draw on together
a tradition that began in India with the Buddha and later spread to China

look.title: Three Neighbors
look.text: Amy's family goes to a Chinese church and also keeps Qingming. Ben's grandmother lights incense at a Buddhist temple. Cindy's family says they have no religion, but they bow to ancestors' photos at New Year.
look.prompt: What do all three families share? What is different for each one?

check.q: What are the three teachings?
check.why: The three teachings are Confucian, Daoist and Buddhist ways of thought.

check.q: Can a family with no religion keep Qingming?
choices: No, it is only for priests
Yes, many families keep it as family custom
Only if they pass an exam
check.why: Many families keep festivals as family custom whether or not they are religious.

check.q: What do scholars debate about Confucianism?
choices: How many zodiac animals there are
check.why: Scholars debate whether Confucianism is a religion or a way of life; views differ.

lessons.title: Visiting With Respect
lessons.mainIdea: Visitors to temples and festivals show respect by watching quietly, asking first and following the host's lead.
reading: Temples welcome visitors, but they are places of worship. People may be praying or making offerings. A respectful *visitor* speaks softly and walks around people who are bowing.
It helps to ask before you take photos, especially of people or altars. Do not touch statues or offerings. If you are not sure what to do, watch quietly or ask a helper at the temple.
At a parade or festival, you can clap, cheer and enjoy the food. Learning a greeting, like "Happy New Year," shows care. Visitors do not have to join any ceremony. Watching with *respect* is enough.

words.d: showing that you value people, places and what matters to them
someone who comes to a place as a guest

look.title: What Would You Do?
look.text: Your class visits a temple. A man is bowing with incense in front of an altar. Your friend lifts a phone to take his picture. A temple helper stands nearby by the door.
look.prompt: What could you or your friend do to show respect here?

check.q: What is a respectful thing to do in a temple?
choices: Take photos of people praying without asking
Speak softly and ask before taking photos
check.why: Visitors show respect by staying quiet and asking before taking photos.

check.q: Do visitors have to join a ceremony?
choices: No; watching with respect is enough
check.why: Visitors may simply watch quietly; they do not have to take part.

check.q: If you are not sure what to do in a temple, what helps?
choices: Watch quietly or ask a helper
Leave the door open and shout
check.why: Watching quietly or asking a temple helper is a respectful way to learn.

review.q: Where is the largest Temple of Confucius?
review.why: The largest Temple of Confucius stands in Qufu, his hometown.

review.q: Which holiday in Taiwan falls on Confucius's traditional birthday?
review.why: Taiwan's Teachers' Day, September 28, is Confucius's traditional birthday.

review.q: Which tradition follows the Dao and honors Laozi?
review.why: Daoism follows the Dao, the Way, and many Daoists honor Laozi.

review.q: What did the civil-service exams test?
review.why: The exams tested the classics, such as the Analects.

review.q: The exams ended in which year?
review.why: China ended its civil-service exams in 1905.

review.q: Which statement about Chinese American families is best?
choices: Many mix traditions, and some keep none
review.why: Chinese American families practice in many ways, and some keep no religion.

review.q: Which is a respectful way to visit a temple?
choices: Watch quietly and ask before photos
Stand in front of someone bowing
review.why: Quiet watching and asking first show respect in a place of worship.

review.q: What does the lion dance bring to shops at New Year?
choices: Good wishes for the new year
review.why: The lion greets each shop and brings good wishes for the new year.
